Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "i’m writing this field notebook entry for the west bench traverse on 18 june, above alder creek in the north fork range. i was the person taking the notes and making the measurements; Elias Ward came with me to carry the sample bags and mark the stops on the route map. We started at 7:40 a.m. from the old forestry gate, at an elevation of about 1,460 metres, with low cloud over the ridge but no rain. The purpose was to check the sandstone contact mapped last autumn and see whether the narrow band could be followed toward the creek. The notebook is mine, although Elias wrote the labels on the sample bags while I called out the station numbers.

The first exposure was a road cut roughly 300 metres east of the gate. I described the sandstone as fine-grained, grey-brown, and mostly in thin beds, with a few rusty streaks along the joints. The bedding dipped 28 degrees toward the southeast, measured with my compass clinometer, and the cut was about six metres high at its tallest point. There were loose blocks at the base, so we stayed on the road shoulder rather than climbing onto the face. Elias held the ranging pole at the lower contact while I checked the angle, then he put a small flag beside the point we used. The flag was orange, not the pink one shown in my older map notes.

At station WB-02, the sandstone gave way to a darker, finer layer that I first called siltstone in my notes. On closer inspection it had a slight sheen and split along very flat surfaces, so I changed the description to shale, not siltstone. I crossed out the first word once and left it readable underneath because I want the correction to show what I thought in the field. The shale layer was about 40 centimetres thick where it was exposed, but the lower edge disappeared beneath moss and gravel. I could not see whether it continued as a single bed around the bend, and I did not measure a contact that was hidden.

Elias collected two pieces from loose material below the cut, and I watched him put them in separate bags rather than combining them. He marked one WB-02A and the other WB-02B, then wrote the date and his initials on both labels. The first piece was a fresh grey chip with a small white vein; the second was weathered brown on one side and had no visible vein. I asked Elias whether either chip had come directly from the bed, and he said, “No, both were already down at the base.” That means the bags are useful examples from the exposure, but they are not samples taken in place.

We followed the contact east for another 180 metres, where alder roots and a shallow ditch interrupted the view. At WB-03 I noted a patch of pale green mineral stain on a joint surface, about the size of my hand. I did not identify the mineral, since the color alone was not enough and I had no hand lens with me that morning. A short distance farther on, the sandstone beds appeared thicker, around 10 to 15 centimetres, though the outcrop was broken and partly covered. Elias measured the distance between the two flagged stops on the map, while I checked the route against the contour lines; our estimate was 180 metres, not a pace count.

The creek crossing was low enough to step over at the marked boulder, but the stones on the north bank were slick. We crossed one at a time, with Elias going first and holding the pack strap while I stepped across. The water was clear and roughly ankle deep at the crossing; I did not take a temperature reading because the thermometer had been left in the vehicle. On the far side, the contact seemed to turn north, but the next 25 metres were hidden by brush. I wrote “possible north turn” in the margin rather than drawing a continuous line. If we return after the brush is cut back, we should check whether the band actually bends north or simply disappears beneath the slope debris.

I also noted the weather because it affects the paper and the exposed surfaces. The cloud lifted around 10:15, and a brief gust dried the wet corners of the map, but the notebook pages stayed dry. The west-facing rock was still damp in the shade, so its darker color may not match the drier face near the road cut. At 11:05, I compared the compass bearing on my field sketch with the route map and found a difference of about five degrees. I have not changed the sketch bearing yet; the compass may have shifted when I set the map beside the metal buckle on my pack. I want to check it away from the pack before treating either bearing as final.

1. WB-01 is the road-cut exposure east of the forestry gate; orange flag placed by Elias at the lower contact.
2. WB-02 is the shale layer in the cut; thickness approximately 40 centimetres where visible, with its lower edge covered.
3. WB-02A and WB-02B are loose pieces collected by Elias below the cut, not in-place samples.
4. WB-03 is the green-stained joint surface farther east; mineral identification remains open.
5. The apparent north turn near the creek is uncertain because brush and slope debris block the view.

I asked Nia Bell, the project archivist, to scan these pages and attach the route map to the same record, rather than filing the map separately. If the notebook paper is still damp when she receives it, I asked her to wait until it is dry before scanning, since the corners curl and the pencil notes are harder to read when they are wet. I have not asked her to interpret the green stain or revise the map. The field sketch includes the three station labels, the orange flag, and the creek crossing, but it does not show the exact position of the two loose sample pieces. Elias’s bag labels and the map should stay with the entry so the sample locations are not mistaken for bedrock collection points.

Before leaving the west bench, we checked the gate-side route once more and found no additional exposure between WB-01 and the gravel pullout. The notebook records the time as 11:40 a.m. when we reached the vehicle, and the sample bags were still separate and dry. I packed the compass in the outer pocket, away from the metal buckle, for the check at the next stop. The final page has a small blank area below the station list for any bearing correction after that check; I have left it blank for now. The creek-side contact remains a field observation to revisit, and the sketch should not be read as proof that the band continues around the bend.", "output": "I’m writing this field notebook entry for the west bench traverse on 18 June, above Alder Creek in the North Fork Range.
